cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 1(a): Arvenia and Belmora are neighbouring coastal states. The small island of Tarn, which undisputedly belongs to Arvenia, lies 8 nautical miles off Arvenia's coast, within Arvenia's territorial sea. Since about 1900, villagers from Belmora's coast have fished every summer around Tarn with small boats and hand-nets; Belmora's fisheries authority issues them annual permits for 'the traditional Tarn fishery'. Arvenia never objected: its coast guard checked the Belmoran boats only for safety, and Arvenia's official fisheries yearbooks repeatedly described the activity as 'the traditional fishing of Belmoran villagers, which Arvenia is bound to respect'. In 2024 Arvenia adopts a law reserving all fishing within 12 nautical miles of Tarn to its own nationals and seizes three Belmoran fishing boats. Belmora claims a customary right of traditional fishing around Tarn. Arvenia replies (1) that customary international law is general law binding all states and cannot arise between two neighbours only, and (2) that it merely tolerated the fishing out of good-neighbourly courtesy. What is customary international law and how does it arise? Assess both of Arvenia's arguments. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Customary international law is a general practice accepted as law; it can also bind just two states, and Arvenia's own yearbooks show a sense of legal obligation, not courtesy — so Belmora very probably has a bilateral customary right of traditional fishing around Tarn.
• Rule: Art 38(1)(b) ICJ Statute; two elements, each to be shown separately (ILC Conclusions on identification of customary international law 2018, Concl. 2): state practice — extensive and virtually uniform, with no minimum duration (North Sea Continental Shelf 1969, para 74) — and opinio iuris, the belief that the practice is legally required. Practice includes verbal acts and, in certain circumstances, inaction (Concl. 6(1)).
• Argument (1) fails: custom may be general, regional (Asylum 1950 — failed only on the evidence) or bilateral: there is no reason why a local custom must involve more than two states (Right of Passage 1960). Particular custom must be accepted as law by EACH state concerned (Concl. 16), and Belmora, which relies on it, must prove that it binds Arvenia (Asylum).
• Practice: the villagers' fishing is private conduct, not itself state practice (Concl. 4(3)); what counts is the conduct of the states — Belmora's permits and Arvenia's tolerance and coast-guard practice, for more than 120 years, every summer, uniform and never contested. Arvenia's failure to react where a reaction was called for is evidence of acceptance as law (Concl. 10(3)); cf. Costa Rica v Nicaragua 2009 (paras 141-144): long, undisturbed subsistence fishing that Nicaragua never denied = customary right of Costa Rica.
• Argument (2) fails: acts done merely out of courtesy, convenience or tradition create no custom (North Sea, para 77) — but official publications are evidence of opinio iuris (Concl. 10(2)), and the yearbooks say Arvenia 'is bound to respect' the fishing: the language of legal duty, not comity.
• Scope and result: the right reaches only as far as the practice — small-scale summer fishing, not industrial fishing (cf. Right of Passage: a right for private persons, civil officials and goods, none for armed forces, which always needed permission). The 2024 law and the seizures breach the bilateral custom.
Memorise: custom = STATE practice (private fishing alone ≠ practice, Concl. 4(3); extensive, virtually uniform, no minimum time — North Sea 74) + opinio iuris (not courtesy — North Sea 77) · general / regional (Asylum) / bilateral (Right of Passage 1960) · particular custom: accepted by EACH state (ILC Concl. 16) · silence where a reaction is expected (Concl. 10(3); Costa Rica v Nicaragua 2009).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 1(b): Arvenia and Belmora are neighbouring coastal states. Since about 1900, villagers from Belmora have fished every summer with small boats in the territorial sea around Arvenia's island of Tarn, without objection from Arvenia. In 1985, replying to a written enquiry from Belmora's ambassador, Arvenia's Foreign Minister stated in an official note that Arvenia 'will never restrict the traditional fishing of Belmoran villagers around Tarn'. Relying on this note, Belmora built a fishing harbour and a fish-processing plant on its coast opposite Tarn. In 2024 Arvenia reserves all fishing within 12 nautical miles of Tarn to its own nationals and seizes three Belmoran fishing boats; Belmora's harbour and plant now stand idle. What is meant by 'general principles of law' in international law, and what is their function? Examine whether Belmora can rely on estoppel and on any other general principle. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: General principles of law (Art 38(1)(c) ICJ Statute) are unwritten principles common to the principal legal systems of the world and transposable to international law, or formed within international law itself, and they serve to fill gaps; Belmora can rely on estoppel — Arvenia's clear representation, on which Belmora relied to its detriment — and also on good faith and the binding force of the minister's declaration.
• Notion: a source next to treaties and custom, but not created by the will of states. Two categories (ILC, Special Rapporteur Vázquez-Bermúdez): principles derived from national legal systems (common to the principal legal systems — comparative method; 'civilized nations' is an outdated phrase — and transposable to the international legal system) and principles formed within the international legal system. Function: gap filling, so that a court need not declare a non liquet. Examples: good faith, estoppel, res judicata, compensation for harm, unjust enrichment, interest for late payment.
• Estoppel (venire contra factum proprium): a statement or representation by one party to another, and reliance on it by that other party to its detriment or to the advantage of the party making it (Land, Island and Maritime Frontier Dispute, ICJ 1990).
• Application: the 1985 note is a clear, unconditional representation by the Foreign Minister to Belmora; Belmora relied on it by building a harbour and a plant that are useless without the fishing → detriment. Arvenia is estopped from denying the traditional fishing.
• Further: the note may itself be a binding unilateral promise — a declaration manifesting the will to be bound creates obligations on the basis of good faith (ILC Guiding Principles 2006, GP 1), and it may be addressed to a single state (GP 6); a foreign minister can bind the state (GP 4; Ihlen declaration, Eastern Greenland, PCIJ 1933; form is not decisive, Nuclear Tests 1974). It is interpreted restrictively — only traditional fishing (GP 7) — and cannot be revoked arbitrarily, especially after the addressee relied on it (GP 10). Arvenia's long silence also amounts to acquiescence.
Memorise: general principles = Art 38(1)(c) · derived from national legal systems + transposition / formed within IL (ILC) · gap filling, no non liquet · estoppel = representation + detrimental reliance (El Salvador/Honduras 1990) · unilateral promise binds on good faith (Eastern Greenland 1933, Nuclear Tests 1974, ILC GP 2006: 1, 4, 6, 7, 10).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 1(c): Since about 1900, villagers from Belmora have fished every summer in the territorial sea around Arvenia's island of Tarn; Arvenia never objected, and its official fisheries yearbooks described this as traditional fishing 'which Arvenia is bound to respect'. In 2024 Arvenia reserves all fishing around Tarn to its own nationals. Arvenia argues: 'Since 1996 both states have been parties to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which gives the coastal state sovereignty over its 12-mile territorial sea and says nothing about traditional fishing there. A treaty always prevails over customary law, and we never consented to a traditional fishing right in any treaty.' Do you agree? Give reasons. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — treaties and custom are of equal rank, custom binds without consent in a treaty, and UNCLOS itself leaves room for the bilateral custom, which would in any case prevail as the special rule.
• No hierarchy among the sources: treaties, custom, general principles, unilateral acts and binding decisions of international organizations stand on the same level; only ius cogens ranks higher (Art 103 UN Charter gives priority only to Charter obligations over other treaties). Conflicts are resolved by interpretation and by lex specialis and lex posterior — a later general rule does not override an earlier special one.
• Custom continues to exist and apply alongside a treaty, even with identical content (Nicaragua 1986, paras 175-179). No treaty consent is needed: a particular custom binds because each state concerned accepted it as law — Arvenia did so by its conduct and its yearbooks.
• No conflict here: under Art 2(3) UNCLOS sovereignty over the territorial sea is exercised subject to the Convention 'and to other rules of international law'; traditional artisanal fishing rights in the territorial sea are vested rights protected through that clause (South China Sea Arbitration, Philippines v China, 2016, para 808).
Memorise: no hierarchy (only ius cogens above) · lex specialis / lex posterior (later general ≠ overrides earlier special) · custom survives alongside a treaty (Nicaragua 175-179) · Art 2(3) UNCLOS 'other rules of international law' · South China Sea 2016: traditional fishing = vested right.

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 2(a): For decades, the southern province of Lusora enjoyed wide autonomy within the State of Corvenia. After a referendum agreed between Corvenia's central government and Lusora's regional parliament, Lusora declared independence on 1 March 2026 with Corvenia's consent. Corvenia keeps its capital, about 85% of its territory and 80% of its population, its armed forces and its diplomatic service, and declares that it continues to exist as the same state. Lusora's new government effectively controls Lusora's territory and population and conducts its own foreign relations; by September 2026, 70 states have recognised Lusora. State Ulmar refuses to recognise Lusora. Ulmar's Foreign Minister declares: 'As long as Ulmar has not recognised Lusora, Lusora is not a state for us. Our warships may therefore enter Lusora's coastal waters whenever they wish, and Lusora cannot complain.' Do you agree? In your answer, explain the criteria of statehood and the legal significance of recognition. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — Lusora is a state because it meets the criteria of statehood; under the prevailing declaratory theory Ulmar's non-recognition does not change this, and Ulmar must respect Lusora's sovereignty and the prohibition of the use of force.
• Criteria (three-elements doctrine; Art 1 Montevideo Convention 1933): a permanent population, a defined territory and an effective, independent government; the capacity to enter into relations with other states is disputed as a criterion (rather a consequence of statehood). Lusora has all three and conducts its own foreign relations. It arose lawfully by consensual secession, so no ius cogens breach triggers a duty of non-recognition (contrast the TRNC 1983).
• Recognition: a unilateral act accepting that an entity is a state. Declaratory theory (prevailing): statehood is a question of fact and recognition only confirms it (Art 3 Montevideo: the political existence of a state is independent of recognition, and even before recognition it may defend its integrity; Badinter Commission, Opinion No. 1, 1991). The constitutive theory would make statehood relative — a state for 70 states, but not for Ulmar. Recognition remains evidence in doubtful cases and the basis of bilateral relations; there is no duty to recognise, so Ulmar may refuse.
• Consequence: Lusora's territorial sea is under its sovereignty; Ulmar's warships may at most exercise the right of innocent passage through it (Art 17 UNCLOS); entering Lusora's internal waters or ports needs its consent. Any other entry violates Lusora's sovereignty, and any threat or use of force violates Art 2(4) UN Charter, which protects 'any state'.
Memorise: Montevideo Art 1: population + territory + effective, independent government [+ capacity — disputed] · recognition declaratory (Montevideo Art 3; Badinter Op. 1), not constitutive · no duty to recognise · non-recognition ≠ licence: Art 2(4) protects 'any state'.

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 2(b): For decades, the southern province of Lusora enjoyed wide autonomy within the State of Corvenia. After an agreed referendum, Lusora declared independence on 1 March 2026 with Corvenia's consent. Corvenia keeps its capital, about 85% of its territory and 80% of its population, its armed forces and its diplomatic service, and declares that it continues to exist as the same state; Lusora's government effectively controls its territory and population, and 70 states have recognised it. Before 1 March 2026, Corvenia was a party to (i) a 1925 treaty with its neighbour Pirnia fixing their common border, which now runs entirely between Lusora and Pirnia; (ii) a bilateral investment treaty (BIT) with State Stavia; (iii) a military alliance with State Mardon; and (iv) the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR). No agreements on these treaties have been made. Classify the succession, name the sources of law applicable to succession in respect of treaties, and determine which of the four treaties bind Lusora and which continue to bind Corvenia. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: This is a secession (separation) with Corvenia continuing as the same state; the border treaty now binds Lusora and no longer Corvenia, the BIT and the ICCPR remain binding on Corvenia and in principle continue for Lusora, and the military alliance stays with Corvenia only.
• Classification: Corvenia keeps its capital, 85% of the territory, 80% of the population, its army and its diplomatic service, claims continuity, and Lusora left by agreement → continuity of Corvenia plus separation of Lusora, not a dismembratio (contrast Czechoslovakia 1993). Only Lusora is a successor state.
• Sources: the 1978 Vienna Convention on Succession of States in respect of Treaties (VCST; in force since 1996, few parties; applies only to successions after its entry into force, Art 7, and only between its parties — the new state Lusora is not one) → customary law, which the VCST partly codifies; in practice also agreements and notifications of succession (a devolution agreement or a unilateral declaration alone does not bind the other treaty parties, Arts 8-9).
• (i) Border treaty: a succession does not as such affect a boundary established by treaty or the boundary regime (Art 11 VCST, customary; a treaty boundary achieves a permanence the treaty itself may lack — Libya/Chad 1994). The boundary binds Lusora; for Corvenia the treaty ceases because it relates only to the separated territory (Art 35(b)).
• (ii) BIT and (iv) ICCPR: Corvenia stays bound for its remaining territory (Art 35). For Lusora, treaties in force for the whole territory continue for each successor (Art 34(1)(a)) unless otherwise agreed or incompatible (Art 34(2)); since the customary status of this rule is uncertain, Lusora and Stavia would confirm the BIT, e.g. by exchange of notes, and Lusora would notify its succession to the ICCPR to the UN Secretary-General. Covenant rights belong to the people and devolve with the territory (Human Rights Committee, General Comment 26, 1997).
• (iii) Military alliance: highly political and tied to the identity of the contracting state — it does not pass to Lusora (cf. Art 34(2)(b)); Corvenia remains bound (Art 35).
Memorise: classify first: continuity + separation · VCST 1978 (Art 7, few parties) + custom + agreements/notifications · borders survive (Art 11; Libya/Chad 1994) · successor: continuity (Art 34, customary status uncertain) · continuing state keeps its treaties except those relating only to the lost territory (Art 35) · alliances never pass · ICCPR: notification + GC 26.

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 2(c): For decades, the southern province of Lusora enjoyed wide autonomy within the State of Corvenia. After an agreed referendum, Lusora declared independence on 1 March 2026 with Corvenia's consent. Corvenia keeps its capital, about 85% of its territory and 80% of its population, and continues to exist as the same state; Lusora is a new state recognised by 70 states. Corvenia and Lusora cannot agree on the division of Corvenia's debts: (i) a loan from the World Bank for a motorway located entirely in Lusora; (ii) a loan granted by State Stavia to finance Corvenia's general state budget; (iii) government bonds issued by Corvenia and held by private investors. Lusora claims that, as a new state, it starts with a 'clean slate' and is not liable for any of these debts. Do you agree? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Largely no — a clean slate for debts exists only for newly independent (formerly dependent) states; in a separation the State debt passes in an equitable proportion unless otherwise agreed; only the private bonds stay with Corvenia, because they are no 'State debt' at all.
• Sources: the 1983 Vienna Convention on Succession of States in respect of State Property, Archives and Debts (VCSSPAD) — not in force, partly customary; an agreement between the states concerned comes first.
• Clean slate: no State debt passes to a newly independent state (Art 38), i.e. a former dependent territory (Art 2(1)(e)). Lusora was an autonomous province, not a colony → no clean slate.
• Separation (Art 40): absent agreement, the State debt passes in an equitable proportion, taking into account in particular the property, rights and interests passing to the successor in relation to that debt. 'State debt' = a financial obligation towards another state, an international organization or another subject of international law (Art 33).
• (i) The World Bank loan (owed to an IO) is State debt; the motorway, immovable property in Lusora, passes to Lusora (Art 17(1)(a)) → this localised debt passes mainly or entirely to Lusora. (ii) Stavia's budget loan has no territorial link → equitable share, e.g. by population or economic capacity (on the dissolution of Czechoslovakia, property and debts were divided 2:1, the population ratio). (iii) Private bonds fall outside Art 33 → custom and agreement; a succession does not as such affect creditors' rights (cf. Art 36), so Corvenia, as issuer and continuing state, remains the debtor; a contribution by Lusora can only be agreed (cf. the 2012 'zero option': Sudan provisionally kept all external debt after South Sudan's secession).
Memorise: VCSSPAD 1983 (not in force) · agreement first · clean slate only for newly independent states (Art 38) · separation = equitable proportion (Art 40), localised debts follow the property (Art 17) · State debt = towards subjects of IL (Art 33) · creditors unaffected (Art 36).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 3(a): All states mentioned are members of the United Nations. In State Lirovia, an armed rebel group, the Northern Liberation Front (NLF), has been fighting the government in two northern provinces since 2025. Lirovia's internationally recognised government asks neighbouring State Kandoria for military help, and Kandoria deploys 2,000 soldiers who fight the NLF. State Drassia, which sympathises with the rebels, supplies the NLF with weapons and trains its fighters in camps on Drassian territory, stating that it is acting at the NLF's request. Assess the lawfulness of (i) Kandoria's military presence in Lirovia and (ii) Drassia's support for the NLF. (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (i) Kandoria's presence is lawful intervention by invitation of the government; (ii) Drassia's arming and training of the NLF is an unlawful use of force and intervention — rebels cannot validly invite foreign states.
• Rule: valid consent of the territorial state's government precludes wrongfulness (Art 20 ARSIWA): the force is not used 'against' that state (Art 2(4) UN Charter) and is no intervention — intervention 'is already allowable at the request of the government' (Nicaragua 1986, para 246). Consent must be freely given, the operation must stay within its scope, and consent can be withdrawn at any time (Armed Activities, DRC v Uganda 2005).
• (i) Kandoria acts at the request of the recognised government against rebels holding two provinces → lawful (cf. France in Mali 2013); debated only where a full civil war is about the people's choice of its government.
• (ii) If the opposition could invite foreign states, nothing would remain of the principle of non-intervention (para 246). Arming and training rebels is an indirect use of force contrary to Art 2(4) and an intervention (para 228; Friendly Relations Declaration 1970); mere funding would be intervention only. Neither amounts to an armed attack (para 195).
Memorise: invitation by the GOVERNMENT = lawful, within scope, revocable (Nicaragua 246; DRC v Uganda 2005; ARSIWA 20) · invitation by REBELS = invalid · arming/training = force (Nicaragua 228), funding = intervention · neither = armed attack.

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 3(b): All states mentioned are members of the United Nations. In State Lirovia, the rebel Northern Liberation Front (NLF) has been fighting the government since 2025; neighbouring State Drassia supplies the NLF with weapons and trains its fighters. In March 2026, Drassia's regular army crosses the border, occupies two Lirovian border towns and shells Lirovian army positions. Lirovia declares that it is the victim of an armed attack, informs the UN Security Council, launches a counter-offensive to retake the two towns and asks the other members of the Southern Defence Pact — a regional alliance of which Lirovia is a member and whose treaty provides for mutual assistance in case of an armed attack — for military help. State Marelia, a Pact member, bombs the Drassian artillery positions and supply routes near the border from which the shelling is conducted. State Venthor, which is not a Pact member and has not been asked for help, bombs government ministries in Drassia's capital, declaring that Drassia 'must be punished'. Assess the lawfulness of the use of force by Lirovia, Marelia and Venthor. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Drassia's invasion and shelling are an armed attack, so Lirovia may defend itself under Art 51 and Marelia may lawfully assist it in collective self-defence at Lirovia's request, within necessity and proportionality; Venthor's punitive strikes are an unlawful armed reprisal in breach of Art 2(4).
• Prohibition: Art 2(4) UN Charter, also customary law and ius cogens; exceptions: self-defence (Art 51) and Security Council measures under Chapter VII.
• Armed attack = the gravest form of the use of force (Nicaragua 1986, para 191), judged by scale and effects (para 195). Invasion, occupation and bombardment by regular forces are acts of aggression (GA Res 3314 (1974), Art 3(a), (b)) and clearly qualify; Drassia's earlier arming and training of the NLF alone would not have sufficed (para 195).
• Lirovia (individual self-defence): the attack is ongoing (occupation) → Lirovia may repel it and retake its towns, within necessity and proportionality (Nicaragua, para 176; Oil Platforms 2003) — the aim is to expel the invader, not to punish; measures must be reported immediately to the Security Council (Art 51), which Lirovia did.
• Marelia (collective self-defence): the victim must declare itself attacked and request assistance; no state may act on its own assessment of the situation (Nicaragua, paras 195, 199). Both conditions are met, and the Pact organises the help in advance (cf. Art 5 NATO Treaty). Striking the artillery and supply routes used for the attack is necessary and proportionate → lawful; Marelia must also report to the Council.
• Venthor: no request → no collective self-defence (Nicaragua, para 199). Punishment is not defence, and armed reprisals are prohibited (Friendly Relations Declaration 1970; Nuclear Weapons AO 1996, para 46); bombing ministries in the capital is neither necessary nor proportionate to repel the attack → violation of Art 2(4).
Memorise: armed attack = gravest force (Nicaragua 191/195; Res 3314 Art 3) · self-defence = armed attack + necessity + proportionality + report to the SC (Art 51) · collective = victim's declaration + REQUEST (Nicaragua 199; alliance = request in advance) · no punishment: armed reprisals unlawful (FRD 1970; Nuclear Weapons 46).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 3(c): State Drassia, a permanent member of the UN Security Council, has armed rebels in neighbouring Lirovia and in March 2026 invaded Lirovia, occupying two border towns. Lirovia is not a member of the Security Council. Two draft resolutions are put to the vote in the Council. Draft 1, a recommendation under Chapter VI calling upon Lirovia and Drassia to settle their dispute by negotiation, receives 13 votes in favour, 1 against (Drassia) and 1 abstention. Draft 2, under Chapter VII, determines a breach of the peace, demands Drassia's immediate withdrawal and imposes an arms embargo on Drassia; it receives 13 votes in favour, 1 against (Drassia) and 1 abstention, cast by another permanent member. Were the drafts adopted? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Draft 1 was adopted, because under Chapter VI Drassia, as a party to the dispute, had to abstain, so its negative vote cannot operate as a veto; Draft 2 failed, because under Chapter VII there is no duty to abstain and Drassia's negative vote is a veto — the other permanent member's abstention is not.
• Rule (Art 27 UN Charter): procedural matters require nine affirmative votes (Art 27(2)); all other matters require nine affirmative votes 'including the concurring votes of the permanent members' (Art 27(3)). Established practice: only an express negative vote of a permanent member is a veto, an abstention is not (Namibia AO 1971, para 22). Proviso of Art 27(3): in decisions under Chapter VI and under Art 52(3), a party to a dispute shall abstain from voting — permanent members included.
• Draft 1: a non-procedural recommendation on peaceful settlement under Chapter VI (Arts 33(2), 36) concerning a dispute to which Drassia is a party → Drassia had to abstain and its 'no' cannot block; 13 ≥ 9, and the abstention (whoever cast it) is no veto → adopted, but only as a non-binding recommendation. (Caveat: the rule is rarely applied in practice, because matters are often treated as 'situations' rather than 'disputes'.) Lirovia is invited to take part in the discussion without a vote (Art 32).
• Draft 2: a Chapter VII decision (Arts 39, 41) → no duty to abstain → Drassia's negative vote is a veto → not adopted despite 13 affirmative votes; no binding arms embargo arises. The General Assembly may then recommend measures (Uniting for Peace, Res 377 (V) 1950), but cannot impose binding sanctions.
Memorise: Art 27(3): 9 'yes' + no P5 'no' · abstention ≠ veto (Namibia 1971) · a party to a dispute must abstain ONLY under Ch VI and Art 52(3) → Draft 1 adopted · Ch VII: the party may vote and veto → Draft 2 fails · GA: recommendations only (377 (V)).

cards.q: Mock exam 2 — Question 3(d): Drassia's regular army invaded neighbouring Lirovia and still occupies two Lirovian towns; Lirovia and its ally Marelia are using force against the Drassian forces in self-defence and have reported this to the UN Security Council. In the Council, Drassia (a permanent member) vetoed a Chapter VII draft demanding its withdrawal and imposing an arms embargo; only a Chapter VI recommendation calling on the parties to negotiate was adopted. Drassia now argues: 'The Security Council is seized of the matter and has adopted a resolution. Lirovia and Marelia must therefore immediately stop all military action.' Do you agree? Give reasons. (1 point)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — under Art 51 the right of self-defence lasts 'until the Security Council has taken measures necessary to maintain international peace and security'; being seized of the matter or adopting a non-binding call to negotiate is no such measure.
• Necessary measures must be capable of restoring peace; Drassia's veto prevented them and cannot extinguish the 'inherent' right (cf. Res 661 (1990): sanctions on Iraq while affirming Kuwait's right of self-defence). Necessity, proportionality and reporting to the Council continue to apply.
Memorise: Art 51 'until the SC has taken measures necessary' · seized / recommendation / veto ≠ necessary measures · Res 661 (1990).
